title: Tools and permissions

story: We wanted a reviewer: a helper session that reads Nova's diff and lists problems, and never changes a file. Someone wrote allowedTools: ["Read", "Grep", "Glob"] and, because nobody sits at a keyboard inside a VM, set the permission mode to bypassPermissions so the session would never stop to ask.

The next morning the reviewer's report said "fixed a typo in ProjectsTable.test.tsx". It had edited a test file, the very thing a reviewer must never do. The list of three tools had not limited anything. It only said which tools could run without asking, and in bypass mode nothing asks anyway.
hook.question: How do I decide, before the session starts, exactly which tools exist, which run freely, and what happens to every other call?

p: Think about setting up a laptop for an intern. First you decide which apps get installed. Then you decide which ones they can open freely and which need your admin password. The SDK asks the same questions about tools, and it has a separate option for each one.

tools is the install list: the built-in tools that exist in this session at all. An array keeps only the names you list, and an empty array removes every built-in tool. allowedTools is the "no password needed" list: calls to these tools are approved without asking. disallowedTools with a plain tool name, such as "Bash", uninstalls a tool so completely that the model never sees it. The trap from the story is that allowedTools installs nothing and removes nothing. A tool that is not in allowedTools still exists, and its calls continue to the next check.

So a reviewer that must never write gets a short tools list, and the model cannot even try Edit, Write or Bash. A builder gets a longer allowedTools list, and the web tools removed. Both are plain objects, so you can test them like any other code.

Approved without asking. Tools not in this list still exist; their calls go to the permission mode.
Plain names: these tools are removed from the request, so the model never sees them.
The install list. The reviewer has three tools in total; Edit, Write and Bash do not exist for it.

read.h: Nobody is at the keyboard: dontAsk
p: Every tool call that the lists do not settle goes to the permission mode. In your terminal, default mode asks you. In a session with nobody watching, asking makes no sense, and the SDK has six modes to choose from. default sends the question to a canUseTool callback in your code, and denies when there is none. acceptEdits approves file edits inside the working folder. plan lets the model explore and never approves an edit by itself. auto lets a second model, a classifier, approve or block each call. bypassPermissions approves everything that reaches it. dontAsk never asks: anything that was not approved in advance is denied.

For agents we always pick dontAsk. It gives a fixed, explicit set of tools, and every refusal is recorded instead of hidden. Calls that need no approval at all, such as reading a file inside the working folder, still run, which is what you want. bypassPermissions is the mode from the story: because it approves everything, allowedTools does not limit it. Set the mode every time, too. If you leave it out, Claude Code chooses a starting mode from the settings files it loads or from its own default, which can be auto.

The order of the checks explains every surprise. For each call, the SDK runs your hooks first, then the deny rules, then any ask rules, then the permission mode, then the allow rules, and last the canUseTool callback. A deny anywhere wins. When a call is refused, the session does not crash: the model reads the refusal and continues, and the result message lists every refusal in permission_denials, with the tool name and its input.

notes.text: The builder's options, but with only read tools approved. Write still exists, so the model may try it.
Every refused call is listed here. A tool that was never installed cannot be refused, because the model never tries it.

p: A plain name approves or removes a whole tool. A scoped rule, a tool name with a pattern in brackets, decides only some calls. Bash(npm test *) approves test runs and nothing else, so other Bash calls still go to the permission mode, where dontAsk denies them. In disallowedTools, Bash(git push *) denies the matching calls but leaves Bash itself installed.

For files, write the rule with Edit, because one Edit(path) rule covers every built-in tool that writes files, Write and NotebookEdit included. A Write(path) rule is never matched by the file checks. Watch the slashes, too: Edit(//etc/**) with two slashes means the real /etc on disk, while a single slash, Edit(/etc/**), is read relative to the session's working folder. It is easy to write a deny rule that looks right and protects nothing.

notes.text: Only these two commands run without asking. Any other Bash call is denied by dontAsk.
A scoped deny: Bash stays installed, but git push never runs. Two slashes in Edit mean an absolute path.

deeper.h: Go deeper: which settings files load, and the system prompt
p: Claude Code also reads permission rules, hooks and skills from settings files: user (~/.claude/settings.json), project (.claude/settings.json in the working folder) and local (.claude/settings.local.json). settingSources picks which of them load. Leave it out and all three load, like the CLI; pass [] and none do. CLAUDE.md files load only when "project" is in the list. Managed settings, the files an administrator controls, load whatever you pass, and your options cannot loosen them.

The system prompt has three shapes. A plain string replaces Claude Code's prompt completely, which suits a judge that should know nothing about editing code. { type: "preset", preset: "claude_code" } keeps Claude Code's own prompt, and adding append: "..." puts your text after it. Nova uses the preset with append, so it keeps Claude Code's knowledge of its tools and adds our guide.

lab.title: A reader, a builder and a test that keeps them honest
needs: For two steps only: your own Anthropic API key
lab.goal: Write tool settings for two roles as plain objects, prove with a test that the reviewer cannot write, and watch a refused call land in permission_denials.

guess.q: A session has allowedTools: ["Read"] and permissionMode: "bypassPermissions". The model asks to run rm -rf build/. What happens?

options.text: It is refused, because Bash is not in allowedTools.
options.why: allowedTools only pre-approves. Bash still exists, and its call goes on to the permission mode.

options.text: It runs, because bypassPermissions approves every call that reaches it.
options.why: That is the warning in the docs: allowedTools does not limit bypassPermissions. Only deny rules, ask rules and hooks would stop it.

options.text: The session pauses and waits for a person to approve.
options.why: Bypass mode never asks. dontAsk never asks either, but it denies instead of approving.

lab.fix: A teammate wants the QA agent to never read the product code in /work/fcp, and writes disallowedTools: ["Read(/work/fcp/**)"]. The session's working folder is /work/.nova/qa. In a test run, the QA agent still read /work/fcp/package.json. Explain why the rule protects nothing, and write the rule that really blocks /work/fcp on disk.
explain: What is the difference between leaving Bash out of allowedTools and putting "Bash" in disallowedTools?
Why do agent sessions use dontAsk and not bypassPermissions, even though both never stop to ask?
A refused call does not crash the session. Where do you find it afterwards, and why is a tool that was never installed missing from that list?
lab.done: Your roles are plain, tested objects, and you can predict for any tool call whether it runs, is refused, or was never possible.

check.q: A reviewer session must never write. Which settings make writing impossible, so the model cannot even try?

options.why: Edit and Write still exist. Their calls go to the permission mode, and in bypass or auto mode they could be approved.
The tools list removes every other built-in tool, so there is nothing to call, and dontAsk denies anything else that would need approval.
Plan mode never auto-approves edits, but it sends them to canUseTool, so whatever answers there decides. And the model still sees the tools and tries them.

check.q: Your options have allowedTools: ["Read", "Glob"] and permissionMode: "bypassPermissions". Can the session run Bash?

options.text: Yes, because bypassPermissions approves every call that is not denied earlier
options.why: allowedTools only pre-approves. It does not limit bypass mode; a deny rule or a hook would be needed to stop Bash.

options.text: No, because Bash is not in allowedTools
options.why: That is the trap from the story. allowedTools is not an install list.

options.text: Only after a person approves it in the terminal

check.q: Why do we set permissionMode explicitly in every agent session?

options.text: Because the SDK refuses to start without it
options.why: It starts fine without one. The problem is which mode it starts in.

options.text: Because dontAsk makes the model faster
options.why: Speed is the same. The mode only decides what happens to calls that need approval.

options.text: Because without it Claude Code picks a starting mode from settings files or its default, which can be auto
options.why: A headless agent needs a fixed, known answer for every call, so we choose dontAsk ourselves.

p: Nova's session approves its working tools (Read, Grep, Glob, Edit, Write, Bash, TodoWrite, the Workflow tool and our own MCP tools) and removes WebFetch and WebSearch, because the egress proxy blocks the web anyway and the model should know that from the start. The mode is always dontAsk, and settingSources is ["project"], so fcp's own CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md and project hooks apply to Nova exactly as they apply to a person.

The self-reviewer gets only Read, Grep and Glob, with no Bash, because git diff --no-index or --output= would let it read or write outside the repo. The QA agent's deny rule for the product code must use the absolute form with two slashes, //work/fcp/**, because its working folder is a different directory. The judges get tools: [] and settingSources: [], so nothing from the repo reaches them.

tickets.why: session.ts is this lesson's options: allowedTools, disallowedTools, dontAsk and settingSources ["project"].
The reviewer gets Read, Grep and Glob only; this lesson explains why Bash is left out.
The QA agent's options use a path deny rule, which needs the two-slash absolute form.
The co-sign session uses tools: [] and settingSources: [].

words.plain: The option that decides which built-in tools exist in the session at all.
Tools whose calls are approved without asking. It removes nothing.
A plain name removes a tool completely; a scoped rule denies only matching calls.
What happens to a call that no list settled: ask, approve, deny, or let a classifier decide.
The mode that never asks: anything not approved in advance is denied and recorded.

review.q: Write the reviewer's options from memory: which three fields, and their values.
review.a: tools ["Read", "Glob", "Grep"], allowedTools with the same three, permissionMode "dontAsk" (and settingSources [] or ["project"] depending on whether repo conventions should apply).

review.q: Give the order in which a tool call is checked.
review.a: Hooks, deny rules, ask rules, permission mode, allow rules, canUseTool. A deny anywhere wins; dontAsk skips canUseTool and denies.

review.q: Why can Edit(/etc/**) in disallowedTools fail to protect /etc?
review.a: One leading slash is relative to the session's working folder. The real /etc on disk needs two slashes: Edit(//etc/**).

remember: tools decides what exists, allowedTools what runs without asking, and dontAsk denies everything else.
